translationRepairs: 列傳第五十八 is the fifty-eighth section of the Biographies, not a year.
He died; posthumously enfeoffed as Palace Attendant, posthumous title Loyal.
He died; posthumously granted the post of Palace Attendant, posthumous title Loyal.
贈侍中 is a posthumous office grant, not an enfeoffment.
His father Datong had served as secretary to the Prince of Yueyang of the Light Chariots guard.
His father Datong had served as secretarial adjutant to the Prince of Yueyang, General of Light Chariots.
輕車岳陽王記室參軍: 輕車 is the prince's general title (General of Light Chariots), not a guard unit; 記室參軍 is a secretarial adjutant.
His father Datong was secretary to the Prince of Yueyang, Light Chariots.
His father Datong was secretary to the Prince of Yueyang, General of Light Chariots.
輕車 abbreviates the prince's title General of Light Chariots (輕車將軍).

During Hou Jing's rebellion he communicated with Wang Huili, heir of Nankang, plotting restoration of the dynasty. When the plot was exposed he was arrested, but the rebel leader Wang Wei protected him and he escaped execution. He then lived as a guest at Jingkou.

During Hou Jing's rebellion he communicated with Huili, Heir Prince of Nankang, plotting restoration of the dynasty. When the plot was exposed he was arrested, but the rebel partisan Wang Wei protected him and he escaped execution. He then lived as a guest at Jingkou.
南康嗣王會理 is Huili, the Heir Prince (嗣王) of Nankang; 王 is part of the title, not a surname. 賊党王偉 is a rebel partisan, not the rebel leader.

During Hou Jing's time he communicated with the Heir of Nankang, Wang Huili, plotting restoration; when the affair was exposed he was arrested; the rebel Wang Wei protected him and he escaped death, then wandered as a guest to Jingkou.

During Hou Jing's time he communicated with the Heir Prince of Nankang, Huili, plotting restoration; when the affair was exposed he was arrested; the rebel Wang Wei protected him and he escaped death, then wandered as a guest to Jingkou.
嗣王 is the title Heir Prince; 會理 is the personal name, with no surname Wang.

When Prince Xian of Hengyang became governor of Wuxing, the emperor, mindful of local elders and the proper order of seniority, feared the young prince might mishandle receptions. He therefore sent Jingli to assist him.

When Chang, Prince Xian of Hengyang, became governor of Wuxing, the emperor, mindful of local elders and the proper order of seniority, feared the young prince might mishandle receptions. He therefore sent Jingli to assist him.
衡陽獻王昌: the idiomatic line omits the prince's personal name 昌 (Chang).

When the Prince of Hengyang, Xian, was Governor of Wuxing, the Emperor, because of local elders and the gradations of senior and junior status, feared the young prince's reception of guests might breach protocol, and sent Jingli to assist him.

When Prince Xian of Hengyang, Chang, was Governor of Wuxing, the Emperor, because of local elders and the gradations of senior and junior status, feared the young prince's reception of guests might breach protocol, and sent Jingli to assist him.
獻 is the prince's posthumous name and 昌 (Chang) his personal name.
When the Chen received the mandate, he was made Director of the Secretariat and Directing Secretariat Clerk, with charge of imperial edicts.
When the Chen received the mandate, he was made Director of the Palace Library and Directing Secretariat Clerk, with charge of imperial edicts.
秘書監 is the director of the Palace Library, as s0285 renders it, not of the Secretariat.
Upon receiving the mandate, he was transferred to Director of the Secretariat and Directing Secretariat Clerk, in charge of edicts.
Upon receiving the mandate, he was transferred to Director of the Palace Library and Directing Secretariat Clerk, in charge of edicts.
秘書監 is the director of the Palace Library, as s0285 renders it, not of the Secretariat.

At that time there were powerful enemies outside; Emperor Wen was stationed at Nangan; the court had no weighty ministers; Empress Xuan called Jingli and Jiang Daquan and Du Ling to decide; they kept the death secret and urgently summoned Emperor Wen.

At that time there were powerful enemies outside; Emperor Wen was stationed at Nanwan; the court had no weighty ministers; Empress Xuan called Jingli and Jiang Daquan and Du Ling to decide; they kept the death secret and urgently summoned Emperor Wen.
南皖 is Nanwan, as in the idiomatic line.

In the fifth year of Taijian (573), supervising Wu Mingche's northern campaign, the army carried all before it, crushing Northern Zhou general Liang Shiyan at Luliang, and was advancing to besiege Pengcheng.

In the fifth year of Taijian (573), Commander-in-Chief Wu Mingche invaded the north, and his army carried all before it, crushing Northern Zhou general Liang Shiyan at Luliang, and was advancing to besiege Pengcheng.
都督吳明徹北侵: 都督 is Wu Mingche's title as commander-in-chief; Cai Jingli did not supervise the campaign.

In the fifth year of Taijian, supervising Wu Mingche's northern invasion, wherever they went they were victorious, utterly defeating Zhou's Liang Shiyan at Luliang, and were advancing to besiege Pengcheng.

In the fifth year of Taijian, Commander-in-Chief Wu Mingche invaded northward; wherever they went they were victorious, utterly defeating Zhou's Liang Shiyan at Luliang, and were advancing to besiege Pengcheng.
都督 is Wu Mingche's title; the subject is Wu Mingche, not Cai Jingli.
When Wu Mingche was defeated, the emperor recalled Jingli's earlier warning and summoned him back that same day, appointing him advisor to the Prince of Poyang on the southern expedition.
When Wu Mingche was defeated, the emperor recalled Jingli's earlier warning and summoned him back that same day, appointing him consultant to the Prince of Poyang, General Who Conquers the South.
征南鄱陽王 is the Prince of Poyang holding the title General Who Conquers the South (征南將軍); there was no 'southern expedition'.
When Wu Mingche was defeated, the Emperor recalled Jingli's earlier words and that same day summoned him back, appointing him Advisor to the Prince of Poyang, Southern Expedition.
When Wu Mingche was defeated, the Emperor recalled Jingli's earlier words and that same day summoned him back, appointing him Consultant to the Prince of Poyang, General Who Conquers the South.
征南 abbreviates the prince's title General Who Conquers the South.

By custom, audiences for new appointments were held in the afternoon. On the day of Jingli's audience, the emperor happened to visit the Xuanyuan Observatory, and all officials in attendance were serving at the banquet. Fearing Jingli would be left out, the emperor specially ordered an early audience. Such was the esteem in which he was held.

By custom, audiences for new appointments were held in the afternoon. On the day of Jingli's audience, the emperor happened to visit the Xuanwu Lodge, and all officials in attendance were serving at the banquet. Fearing Jingli would be left out, the emperor specially ordered an early audience. Such was the esteem in which he was held.
玄武觀 is the Xuanwu Lodge (玄武), not 'Xuanyuan', and a palace lodge rather than an observatory.

The old custom for appointment audiences was after noon; on the day of Jingli's audience, it happened the imperial carriage visited the Xuanyuan Observatory; all in office were attending the banquet; the Emperor feared Jingli would not be included and specially ordered an early audience—such was the esteem in which he was held.

The old custom for appointment audiences was after noon; on the day of Jingli's audience, it happened the imperial carriage visited the Xuanwu Lodge; all in office were attending the banquet; the Emperor feared Jingli would not be included and specially ordered an early audience—such was the esteem in which he was held.
玄武觀 is the Xuanwu Lodge (玄武), not 'Xuanyuan', and a palace lodge rather than an observatory.
He died in office and was posthumously made Minister of Rites, with the posthumous name Respectful.
He died in office and was posthumously made Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, with the posthumous name Respectful.
太常卿 is the chief minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, not Minister of Rites.
He died in office; posthumously enfeoffed as Minister of Rites, posthumous title Respectful.
He died in office; posthumously granted the post of Chief Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, posthumous title Respectful.
贈太常卿 is a posthumous office grant (not an enfeoffment) of chief minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices.
In the thirteenth year, on reburial he was again posthumously enfeoffed as General-in-Chief of the Center.
In the thirteenth year, on reburial he was again posthumously granted the post of General-in-Chief of the Center.
重贈中領軍 is a posthumous office grant, not an enfeoffment.

In the second year, the emperor personally visited his former residence, again posthumously enfeoffing Jingli as Palace Attendant and General Who Pacifies the Center, with the posthumous name Loyal and Respectful, granting a set of ceremonial music, and erecting a stele at his tomb.

In the second year, the emperor personally visited his former residence, again posthumously granting Jingli the posts of Palace Attendant and General Who Pacifies the Center, with the posthumous name Loyal and Respectful, granting a set of ceremonial music, and erecting a stele at his tomb.
重贈 grants posthumous offices; it is not an enfeoffment.

In the second year, the imperial carriage personally visited his residence, again posthumously enfeoffing Jingli as Palace Attendant and General Who Pacifies the Center, posthumous title Loyal and Respectful, granting a set of ceremonial music, and erecting a stele at the tomb.

In the second year, the imperial carriage personally visited his residence, again posthumously granting Jingli the posts of Palace Attendant and General Who Pacifies the Center, posthumous title Loyal and Respectful, granting a set of ceremonial music, and erecting a stele at the tomb.
重贈 grants posthumous offices; it is not an enfeoffment.
He was soon appointed Director of the Left Household Department and, together with Vice Minister Jiang Zong, oversaw compilation of the Five Rites.
He was soon appointed Director of the Left Household Department and, together with Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Jiang Zong, oversaw compilation of the Five Rites.
僕射 is the vice director of the Department of State Affairs, not a 'vice minister'.
His son Yi served as secretary to the Minister of State Affairs.
His son Yi served as secretary to the Minister over the Masses (Situ).
司徒 is the Minister over the Masses (Situ), one of the three dukes, not a 'Minister of State Affairs'.
Rated highest in his performance review, he was summoned to court and by edict made Supernumerary Regular Attendant-at-Court.
Rated highest in his performance review, he was summoned to court and by edict made Regular Attendant-at-Court.
The text has 散騎常侍 (regular attendant) without 員外 (supernumerary).
Soon appointed Director of the Left Household Department, together with Vice Minister Jiang Zong overseeing composition of the Five Rites.
Soon appointed Director of the Left Household Department, together with Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Jiang Zong overseeing composition of the Five Rites.
僕射 is the vice director of the Department of State Affairs, not a 'vice minister'.
His son Yi held the post of Secretary to the Minister of State Affairs.
His son Yi held the post of Secretary to the Minister over the Masses (Situ).
司徒 is the Minister over the Masses (Situ), one of the three dukes, not a 'Minister of State Affairs'.
Because of top marks in assessment he entered court; an edict added Supernumerary Regular Attendant-at-Court.
Because of top marks in assessment he entered court; an edict added Regular Attendant-at-Court.
The text has 散騎常侍 (regular attendant) without 員外 (supernumerary).
When the secretariat of Minister of State Affairs Wang Sengbian was first established, Yuanrao and Liu Shizhi of Pei both served as chief clerks.
When the headquarters of Minister over the Masses Wang Sengbian was first established, Yuanrao and Liu Shizhi of Pei both served as chief clerks.
司徒王僧辯幕府 is the headquarters (幕府) of Wang Sengbian as Minister over the Masses (司徒).
When the Secretariat of Wang Sengbian, Minister of State Affairs, was first established, Yuanrao and Liu Shizhi of Pei were both chief clerks.
When the headquarters of Wang Sengbian, Minister over the Masses, was first established, Yuanrao and Liu Shizhi of Pei were both chief clerks.
幕府 is a headquarters, and 司徒 is the Minister over the Masses.

Wang Boli, Prince of Wuling and governor of Wuxing, Wang Fangtai, heir of Nankang and interior administrator of Yuzhang, and others were arrogant and overbearing. Yuanrao investigated and memorialized against them, and all were demoted.

Boli, Prince of Wuling and governor of Wuxing, Fangtai, Heir Prince of Nankang and interior administrator of Yuzhang, and others were arrogant and overbearing. Yuanrao investigated and memorialized against them, and all were demoted.
武陵王伯禮 and 南康嗣王方泰: 王 belongs to the titles Prince (王) and Heir Prince (嗣王); Boli and Fangtai are personal names, not surnamed Wang.

Governor of Wuxing, Prince of Wuling Wang Boli, Interior Administrator of Yuzhang, Heir of Nankang Wang Fangtai, and others were arrogant and unrestrained; Yuanrao investigated and memorialized; all were demoted.

Governor of Wuxing, Prince of Wuling Boli, Interior Administrator of Yuzhang, Heir Prince of Nankang Fangtai, and others were arrogant and unrestrained; Yuanrao investigated and memorialized; all were demoted.
王 belongs to the titles; Boli and Fangtai have no surname Wang.

After Hou Jing was defeated, Chen Wendi went out to take charge of Wuxing. Zigao was sixteen, just come of age, with a beautiful face that looked almost feminine. At a crossing on the Huai he had joined a convoy hoping to return home. Wendi saw him and asked, "Will you serve me?"

After Hou Jing was defeated, Chen Wendi went out to take charge of Wuxing. Zigao was sixteen, still wearing a boy's hair tufts, with a beautiful face that looked almost feminine. At a crossing on the Huai he had joined a convoy hoping to return home. Wendi saw him and asked, "Will you serve me?"
為總角 means he still wore his hair in a boy's tufts (not yet capped), not that he had come of age.

When Jing was pacified, Chen Wen went out to guard Wuxing; Zigao was sixteen, in the coming-of-age years, beautiful in appearance, his form resembling a woman's; at the Huai ford he attached to a unit for passage wishing to return home; Wen saw him and asked: "Can you serve me?"

When Jing was pacified, Chen Wen went out to guard Wuxing; Zigao was sixteen, wearing a boy's hair tufts, beautiful in appearance, his form resembling a woman's; at the Huai ford he attached to a unit for passage wishing to return home; Wen saw him and asked: "Can you serve me?"
總角 denotes a boy's tufted hair, i.e. not yet of age.
When the new emperor took the throne, Zigao was given the additional title of Regular Attendant-at-Court.
When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Zigao was given the additional title of Regular Attendant-at-Court.
廢帝 is the Deposed Emperor (a standard designation), not 'the new emperor'.
When the deposed emperor's successor took the throne, he was given the additional post of Regular Attendant-at-Court.
When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, he was given the additional post of Regular Attendant-at-Court.
廢帝即位 means the Deposed Emperor himself took the throne, not his successor.
When the new emperor took the throne, Jiao was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Chong'an county.
When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, Jiao was re-enfeoffed as Duke of Chong'an county.
廢帝 is the Deposed Emperor, not 'the new emperor'.
When the new emperor took the throne, his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Chong'an county.
When the Deposed Emperor took the throne, his enfeoffment was changed to Duke of Chong'an county.
廢帝 is the Deposed Emperor, not 'the new emperor'.
That same night he was executed along with Dao Zhongju.
That same night he was ordered to take his own life along with Dao Zhongju.
賜死 is being granted (ordered to take) death, not a public execution.
Liang Mingdi sent a fleet in support of Jiao. Northern Zhou Wudi sent Duke of Wei Yuwen Zhi to hold Lushan and Pillar of State Xi Yuanding of Changhu to besiege Ying province.
Liang Mingdi sent a fleet in support of Jiao. Northern Zhou Wudi sent Duke of Wei Yuwen Zhi to hold Lushan and Pillar of State Yuan Ding of Changhu to besiege Ying province.
柱國長湖西元定: the man is Yuan Ding (元定, as s0142 calls him); 長湖 is his fief, and 西 is not a surname (external histories give him as Duke of Changhu, 長湖公).

At that time Liang Ming Di sent a navy as vocal support for Jiao; Zhou Wu Di sent Duke of Wei Yuwen Zhi stationed at Lushan, and also sent Pillar of State Xi Yuanding of Changhu to attack and besiege Ying Prefecture.

At that time Liang Ming Di sent a navy as vocal support for Jiao; Zhou Wu Di sent Duke of Wei Yuwen Zhi stationed at Lushan, and also sent Pillar of State Yuan Ding of Changhu to attack and besiege Ying Prefecture.
The person is Yuan Ding (元定); 西 is not his surname.
Yuanding and his men could no longer cross by ship and marched overland toward Baling, but the city was already held by Chen forces. They surrendered and were sent to Jianye.
Yuan Ding and his men could no longer cross by ship and marched overland toward Baling, but the city was already held by Chen forces. They surrendered and were sent to Jianye.
元定 is Yuan Ding: surname Yuan (元), given name Ding.
In the first year of Tiankang, when Wendi fell ill, Shizhi entered with Vice Minister Dao Zhongju and others to attend him with medicines.
In the first year of Tiankang, when Wendi fell ill, Shizhi entered with Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Dao Zhongju and others to attend him with medicines.
尚書僕射 is the vice director of the Department of State Affairs.
Yuanding and others had no more boats to cross; they went on foot toward Baling; Baling city was already held by Chen troops; they then surrendered and were sent to Jianye.
Yuan Ding and others had no more boats to cross; they went on foot toward Baling; Baling city was already held by Chen troops; they then surrendered and were sent to Jianye.
元定 is Yuan Ding: surname Yuan (元), given name Ding.
In the first year of Tiankang, when Wen was unwell, Shizhi together with Vice Minister of State Affairs Dao Zhongju and others entered to attend with medicine.
In the first year of Tiankang, when Wen was unwell, Shizhi together with Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs Dao Zhongju and others entered to attend with medicine.
尚書僕射 is the vice director of the Department of State Affairs.
Shizhi's original name had been Shizhi, identical to the taboo name of Emperor Jing of Liang, and was therefore changed.
Shizhi's original name had been Shizhi (師智), identical to the taboo name of Emperor Jing of Liang, and was therefore changed.
The original name 師智 is homophonous with 師知; without the characters the sentence reads as if the name did not change.

When Xuandi entered as regent, Shizhi and Zhongju sent Clerk Yin Buniu with a forged edict ordering Xuandi back to the Eastern Residence. When the plot was exposed, Shizhi was executed in the northern prison.

When Xuandi entered as regent, Shizhi and Zhongju sent Clerk Yin Buning with a forged edict ordering Xuandi back to the Eastern Residence. When the plot was exposed, Shizhi was ordered to die in the northern prison.
殷不佞 is read Yin Buning (佞 ning); 賜死 means being ordered to take one's life, not execution.

When Xuandi entered as regent, Shizhi with Zhongju and others sent Clerk Yin Buniu with a forged edict ordering Xuandi to return to the Eastern Residence; when the affair was exposed, he was granted death in the northern prison.

When Xuandi entered as regent, Shizhi with Zhongju and others sent Clerk Yin Buning with a forged edict ordering Xuandi to return to the Eastern Residence; when the affair was exposed, he was granted death in the northern prison.
佞 is read ning: Yin Buning.
In the first year of Yongding he was made Gentlemen Attendant of the Yellow Gates and Directing Secretariat Clerk, retaining his concurrent post as right assistant minister.
In the first year of Yongding he was made Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates and Directing Secretariat Clerk, retaining his concurrent post as right assistant minister.
給事黃門侍郎 is a single office holder: Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates (singular).
When the emperor took the throne, Xi was appointed Gentlemen Attendant of the Yellow Gates and concurrently Directing Secretariat Clerk, in charge of military and state secrets.
When the emperor took the throne, Xi was appointed Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates and concurrently Directing Secretariat Clerk, in charge of military and state secrets.
給事黃門侍郎 is Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates (singular).
His grandfather Cheng had been Regular Attendant under the Liang.
His grandfather Cheng had been Gentleman Cavalier Attendant under the Liang.
散騎侍郎 is a gentleman cavalier attendant, distinct from 散騎常侍 (regular attendant).
His father Qizhong had been marshal of the Central Guard.
His father Qizhong had been adjutant to the General of the Central Authority.
中權司馬 is the adjutant (司馬) of the General of the Central Authority (中權將軍), not a marshal of a guard.

On his mother's death he left office. An edict enfeoffed Xi's mother, Lady Yu, as Grand Lady of Dongchang State, sent Extraordinary Attendant Du Mian to survey her tomb fields, and the emperor personally traced the map with Mian. Such was the esteem in which Xi was held.

On his mother's death he left office. An edict enfeoffed Xi's mother, Lady Yu, as Grand Lady of Dongchang State, sent Supernumerary Regular Attendant-at-Court Du Mian to survey her tomb fields, and the emperor personally traced the map with Mian. Such was the esteem in which Xi was held.
員外散騎常侍 is rendered Supernumerary Regular Attendant-at-Court elsewhere in the chapter.
He served successively as Inspector-in-Chief and Minister of the Five Armies and participated in managing appointments.
He served successively as Censor-in-Chief and Minister of the Five Armies and participated in managing appointments.
御史中丞 is the Censor-in-Chief, as rendered elsewhere in the chapter.
In the first year of Yongding, he was made Gentlemen Attendant of the Yellow Gates and Directing Secretariat Clerk, retaining his concurrent post as right assistant minister.
In the first year of Yongding, he was made Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates and Directing Secretariat Clerk, retaining his concurrent post as right assistant minister.
給事黃門侍郎 is a single office holder: Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates (singular).
When the emperor took the throne, Xi was appointed Gentlemen Attendant of the Yellow Gates and concurrently Directing Secretariat Clerk, in charge of military and state secrets.
When the emperor took the throne, Xi was appointed Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates and concurrently Directing Secretariat Clerk, in charge of military and state secrets.
給事黃門侍郎 is Gentleman Attendant of the Yellow Gates (singular).
His grandfather Cheng was Regular Attendant under the Liang.
His grandfather Cheng was Gentleman Cavalier Attendant under the Liang.
散騎侍郎 is a gentleman cavalier attendant, distinct from 散騎常侍 (regular attendant).
His father Qizhong was Marshal of the Central Guard.
His father Qizhong was adjutant to the General of the Central Authority.
中權司馬 is the adjutant (司馬) of the General of the Central Authority (中權將軍), not a marshal of a guard.

On his mother's death he left office; an edict enfeoffed Xi's mother, Lady Yu, as Grand Lady of Dongchang State, sent Extraordinary Attendant Du Mian to survey her tomb fields, and the emperor personally traced the map with Mian—such was the esteem in which Xi was held.

On his mother's death he left office; an edict enfeoffed Xi's mother, Lady Yu, as Grand Lady of Dongchang State, sent Supernumerary Regular Attendant-at-Court Du Mian to survey her tomb fields, and the emperor personally traced the map with Mian—such was the esteem in which Xi was held.
員外散騎常侍 is rendered Supernumerary Regular Attendant-at-Court elsewhere in the chapter.
He served successively as Inspector-in-Chief, Minister of the Five Armies, and participated in managing appointments.
He served successively as Censor-in-Chief, Minister of the Five Armies, and participated in managing appointments.
御史中丞 is the Censor-in-Chief, as rendered elsewhere in the chapter.

When Wendi died, the young emperor was still a child. Xuandi took charge of the Ministry of State Affairs as regent. Vice Minister Dao Zhongju and others forged an order from the empress dowager sending Xuandi back to the Eastern Residence. Everyone was fearful, and no one dared speak.

When Wendi died, the Deposed Emperor was young and unfit to rule. Xuandi took charge of the Ministry of State Affairs as regent. Vice Director Dao Zhongju and others forged an order from the empress dowager sending Xuandi back to the Eastern Residence. Everyone was fearful, and no one dared speak.
廢帝沖昧 names the Deposed Emperor (廢帝) as young and benighted; 僕射 is the vice director of the Department of State Affairs.

When Wen died, the young emperor was immature; Xuan took charge of the Ministry of State Affairs as regent; Vice Minister Dao Zhongju and others forged the Empress Dowager's order sending Xuan back to the Eastern Residence; at the time all were doubtful and fearful, none daring to speak.

When Wen died, the Deposed Emperor was young and benighted; Xuan took charge of the Ministry of State Affairs as regent; Vice Director Dao Zhongju and others forged the Empress Dowager's order sending Xuan back to the Eastern Residence; at the time all were doubtful and fearful, none daring to speak.
廢帝 is the Deposed Emperor; 僕射 is a vice director, not a vice minister.

At that time the crown prince loved wine and virtue; he often with favored intimates held all-night banquets; Xi once spoke of this to Xuan; the crown prince therefore harbored resentment; after taking the throne he was gradually seen at a distance.

At that time the crown prince was fond of drinking (the 'virtue of wine'); he often with favored intimates held all-night banquets; Xi once spoke of this to Xuan; the crown prince therefore harbored resentment; after taking the throne he was gradually seen at a distance.
好酒德 means fond of drinking (酒德, the 'virtue of wine'), not wine and virtue.
He then plotted with Sima Shen, saying, "This man is proud. I want to send him to the brothers of Poyang and let him take his revenge. Would that do?"
He then plotted with Sima Shen, saying, "This man is proud. I want to hand him over to the brothers of Poyang and let them take their revenge on him. Would that do?"
乞鄱陽兄弟，聽其報讎: Mao Xi would be handed to the Poyang brothers so that they could take revenge on him, not he on them.
He then plotted with Sima Shen, saying: "This man is proud in spirit; I wish to send him to beg the brothers of Poyang and let him take revenge—may I?"
He then plotted with Sima Shen, saying: "This man is proud in spirit; I wish to give him to the brothers of Poyang and let them take revenge—may I?"
乞 here means to give (hand over); 其 refers to the Poyang brothers taking revenge.
When they returned and were about to bury him, an edict posthumously enfeoffed Xun as Palace Attendant and General Who Leads the Army, posthumous title Respectful.
When they returned and were about to bury him, an edict posthumously granted Xun the posts of Palace Attendant and General Who Leads the Army, posthumous title Respectful.
贈 grants posthumous offices; it is not an enfeoffment.
Xuandi made Junli's daughter crown princess, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wangcai county, and appointed him Palace Attendant and Right Vice Minister of State Affairs.
Xuandi made Junli's daughter crown princess, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Wangcai county, and appointed him Palace Attendant and Right Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs.
尚書右僕射 is the right vice director of the Department of State Affairs.
In Wenyü's southern campaign, which defeated Xiao Bo and captured Ouyang Yu, most of the plans came from Shancai.
In Wenyü's southern campaign, which defeated Xiao Bo and captured Ouyang Wei, most of the plans came from Shancai.
歐陽頠 is read Ouyang Wei (頠 wei).
When Chen fell he entered Sui service, but Emperor Wen ordered him executed at Jianye for his earlier defection.
When Chen fell he entered Sui service, but Emperor Wen ordered him executed at Jiankang for his earlier defection.
建康 is Jiankang; the text does not say Jianye here.
When Wenyü was again stationed at Jinkou in Yuzhang, Shancai again served as chief clerk of the southern garrison and governor of Yuzhang.
When Wenyü was again stationed at Jinkou in Yuzhang, Shancai again served as chief administrator to the General Who Guards the South and governor of Yuzhang.

unresolvedReferences.description: The packet supplies no reign table. External Liang/Chen conversions: Chengsheng AD 552–555, Yongding 1 = AD 557, Tianjia 1 = AD 560, Taijian 1 = AD 569; event dates (Yuan Jingzhong AD 549, Hou Jing AD 548–552, Wang Sengbian AD 555, Wang Lin AD 560, Hou Andu AD 563, Hua Jiao AD 567, accessions of Wendi AD 559 and Xuandi AD 569) are external.

External identifications: Emperor Wu of Chen = Chen Baxian; Emperor Wen = Chen Qian; Emperor Xuan = Chen Xu; Emperor Yuan of Liang = Xiao Yi; the Prince of Yueyang = Xiao Cha; Huili of Nankang = Xiao Huili; Prince Xian of Hengyang = Chen Chang; Empress Xuan (宣後, for 宣后) = Zhang Yao'er.

Han Zigao, Liu Shizhi, Xie Qi, Mao Xi, Shen Junli and Lu Shancai appear in this chunk only in the chapter heading; their biographies fall in later chunks, and their active-date hints here are broad external Chen-dynasty bounds.

帝 in s0045 and s0047 is Emperor Xuan (named in read-only s0039/s0041 and in owned s0093); the emperor whose carriage visits in s0051 (Zhenming 2) is taken as the Later Lord (strongly inferred). No reign table in the packet: Taijian 1 = AD 569, Zhide 1 = AD 583, Zhenming 1 = AD 587 are external conversions; Wu Mingche's defeat and Cai Jingli's death in AD 578 are external dates.

External identifications: Prince of Poyang = Chen Boshan; Later Lord = Chen Shubao; Emperor Wen of Sui = Yang Jian; Boli of Wuling = Chen Boli; Fangtai of Nankang = Chen Fangtai; the crown prince of s0067 is uncertain (Chen Yin or Chen Shen). Wang Xiang (s0061) is the Wei–Jin filial exemplar, recalled only as a model.

No reign table in the packet: Tianjia 1 = AD 560 and Guangda 1 = AD 567 are external conversions; Hou Jing (AD 548–552), Du Kan and Zhang Biao (AD 555–556), Wendi's accession (AD 559) and death (AD 566), Wang Lin (AD 559–560) and Zhou Di (AD 563–565) are external dates.

External identifications: Wendi = Chen Qian; Wudi = Chen Baxian; Xuandi = Chen Xu; the Deposed Emperor (廢帝) = Chen Bozong; the crown prince whose installation was debated in s0124 = Chen Zhize; Emperor Ming of Liang = Xiao Kui of the Western Liang. The commander (軍主) who accused Han Zigao is an unnamed role and is not given a person record.

s0137–s0143 continue the Guangda 1 (AD 567, external conversion) narrative of Hua Jiao's rebellion from read-only s0132. 長湖西元定 is taken as Yuan Ding (元定, as in s0142) of Changhu; external histories give him as Duke of Changhu (長湖公), so 西 may be a textual corruption. The emperor (帝) of s0140 is taken as Xuandi (strongly inferred; the reigning Deposed Emperor is not named here).

No reign table in the packet: Shaotai 1 = AD 555, Yongding 1 = AD 557, Tianjia 1 = AD 560, Tiankang 1 = AD 566 are external conversions; Emperor Jing's killing (AD 558), Wudi's accession (AD 557) and death (AD 559), and the forged-edict plot (AD 566–567) are external dates. External identifications: Emperor Jing = Xiao Fangzhi; Emperor Wu of Zhou = Yuwen Yong; Emperor Ming of Liang = Xiao Kui; Crown Prince Zhaoming = Xiao Tong (AD 501–531); Fu Xuan (AD 217–278) and Wang Shang (Western Han chancellor, before 25 BC) are allusions.

The crown prince (皇太子/太子) of s0213 is the future Later Lord (後主), as the passage itself continues (即位後); the Prince of Shixing (始興王) of s0214 is taken as Chen Shuling (叔陵) of s0208 (external identification). The emperor (帝/上) of s0204, s0205, s0211, s0309 and s0312 is Xuandi.

No reign table in the packet: Yongding 1 = AD 557, Tianjia 1 = AD 560 are external conversions; the fall of Jiangling (AD 554), Wendi's accession (AD 559) and death (AD 566), Xuandi's return (AD 562), accession (AD 569) and death (AD 582), Wu Mingche's capture (AD 578) and Shuling's revolt (AD 582) are external dates. External identifications: Empress Liu = Liu Jingyan; the empress dowager of s0196 = Shen Miaorong; Emperor Yuan of Liang = Xiao Yi; Later Lord = Chen Shubao. Du Shuying and Yu Shuqing are ancient worthies cited only as name models.

The crown prince (皇太子) of s0243 is the future Later Lord (後主, s0250), strongly inferred from Xuandi's reign; the emperor (帝) of s0235 is Chen Wudi; 文帝 in s0237 is Emperor Wen of Chen but in s0252 Emperor Wen of Sui. External identifications: Emperor Yuan of Liang = Xiao Yi; Emperor Xuan of Liang = Xiao Cha; Later Lord = Chen Shubao; Emperor Wen of Sui = Yang Jian; Junli's daughter = Shen Wuhua.

No reign table in the packet: Shaotai 1 = AD 555, Tianjia 1 = AD 560, Tiankang 1 = AD 566, Taijian 1 = AD 569, Zhide 1 = AD 583, Zhenming 1 = AD 587 are external conversions; the fall of Jingzhou (AD 554), the Xiao Bo campaign (AD 557), Zhou Wenyu's death (AD 559), Shen Junli's death (AD 573), the Xiao Huan defection (AD 587) and the fall of Chen (AD 589) are external dates. The closing appraisal (s0266–s0275) recalls Zhao Zhili, Cai Jingli, Cai Zheng (by courtesy name 希祥), Zong Yuanrao, Han Zigao, Hua Jiao, Liu Shizhi, Mao Xi, Shen Junli and Lu Shancai (the last two by surname alone), and compares Fu Liang (AD 374–426) and Wang Jian (AD 452–489).
